To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the cost of collecting the additional information needed to target candidates for school-based preventive interventions more effectively is likely to be justified when the cost of collecting that information is less than the cost of implementing an intervention for candidates for whom the expected benefits are less than those expected for the average candidate, and when the cost of implementing the intervention is more than the cost of collecting and using additional information to target candidates for whom the benefits of the intervention are more than those expected for average candidates; (2)
the expected net benefits of a preventive intervention may be maximized through screening to identify high-risk children, but the cost of screening must be weighed against the potential benefits.

(1) the cost of collecting information about candidates for school based intervention is not likely to be justified by the resulting increase in economic net benefit if the intervention is effective and the cost of the information is small relative to the cost of the intervention; and, (2) the cost of information collection is more likely to be justified if the intervention is ineffective and the cost of information is small relative the cost of the ineffective intervention.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of when it is cost-effective to use more information about candidates to target interventions to those most likely to benefit.
how the economic value of information for screening in disseminating and targeting effective school based preventive interventions can be estimated.

the economic value of information for targeting in school based preventive interventions is likely to be positive, and that the magnitude of this value is sensitive to the magnitude of the expected benefits of the intervention.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the results of our illustrative example indicate that the expected economic value of information (EVI) for targeting is likely to be positive, but not large.
the economic value of additional information for targeting is likely to be substantial, but the magnitude of this value is likely to be sensitive to the cost of collecting information.

the economic value of information for screening is likely to be positive in most circumstances, but that the value depends on the cost of the screening test, the cost of the effective intervention, the cost of collecting the information needed to implement the screening test, and the accuracy with which the screening test predicts who will and will not benefit from the intervention.
The main takeaway from our work is that

cost benefit analysis results can provide useful information for deciding how much additional information is needed to make more accurate targeting decisions, and that the results are likely to be sensitive to the assumptions used.

, in the absence of a clear answer to this question, it may be prudent to collect more information than we would otherwise collect, and to use the results from our cost benefit analysis to inform the design of the information gathering process.
